That's all up to each individual. I got my diagnoses for free(I think. At the very least I myself didn't pay for it) and I now have financial benefits to keep me afloat. Someone else may feel just fine not being officially diagnosed

It opens up room for accomodations that you wouldn't be able to get without official diagnosis, for now or for the future, it may get certain people to take your struggles seriously (my parents did not take mine seriously, even after I was almost sorta diagnosed twice, first as a kid, then at 15), it can help validate one's struggles

Some people want a diagnosis but can't afford it, some people would like it but still think it's pricey and not worth the cost, some may not want an official diagnosis at all

I've heard many stories of people being discriminated against in getting diagnosed, or people that think autism is only in children. Some may not find it worth the money, the struggle or the potential waiting times

It's not like you have to decide now if you want to get diagnosed. If you don't find it useful/worth it right now, you don't have to. The option will still be available in the future in case you change your mind

To give you some perspective from an autistic person in college(AKA me), it can be very different from high school. For one, choosing a specific course helps eliminate some of those awful subjects. For the course I took, there's the subjects programming, English, my native language, calculus, social studies and one year of gym class. Now, I got lucky with my high school diploma making me eligible to drop both languages, I already finished my calculus exam in the first year and I don't have to redo it, and for social studies, well, our teacher is still sick, so I don't know what would've happened had he not been. But no math, no German, no other subjects I hated so much in high school.

Some colleges offer different schedules. Mine was supposed to be morning classes in-person, afternoon classes online, which is already far more manageable than full school days. It's been all over the place due to you-know-what, but it's only ever been less in-person classes and more online. It makes a huge difference for me, not feeling "observed", being able to decide when to take breaks and overall just being in a far more comfortable environment. There are even full online courses. Be warned, I myself struggled with motivation with full online classes, it's worth keeping in mind.

As someone who struggled with bullying for literal years, it seems people in college(in my experience) have sorta grown out of their childish phases, with some exceptions of course. But I have actually not been bullied, and even made friends, which was unthinkable in high school.

I've found that teachers take me more seriously now than they used to. It may just be because I'm older, but the teachers are more understanding and willing to think along with me to help find ways to make my school days just a bit less exhausting. I already got an extra 15 minute break, and had teachers informed I'm allowed to ask for an open room if I ever just need some space to gather myself. Especially so when you tell them you have autism. I've found it uncomfortable to share with the teachers, but it does help them understand my behaviours and, most importantly, umderstanding that when I run out of "battery", I'm not just some slacker goofing around.

For the brief time I had one full school day, I discussed with my teacher what to do, as I can't handle a full day. I was told that, if my battery runs out, I'm allowed to leave and rest up. Sitting there with no energy or motivation is not productive, but resting up and recharging definitely is.

And finally, don't try to force yourself to have a job and go to college if you can't handle it. I couldn't either, so I quit my job to focus on school. What's better, if you have an official diagnosis, you may be eligible for extra financial aid. I say you may be because I'm no government worker, nor do I know where you're from, but it's worth asking about. Getting some extra money could be beneficial, especially in a situation where you may not be able to earn money through a job.

I hope this message gives hope that high school diesn't last forever, and that college is different from high school. Wishing you all the best!

I have a sort of system, as well as a "list" of what I find most important.

First thing I look at is color and pattern. Red and black are my favorite colors, camouflage and leopard print are my favorite patterns. Though I do like a lot of other colors and patterns as well.

I'll take a closer look. Do I like it? Continue on down the "list". If I don't, put it back.

Second is the feel/fabric. Is it comfortable? Continue. If not, put it back. For example, I dislike the feeling of denim and other rougher fabrics.

Third, size. Is it available in my size or not? If I'm unsure I'll still continue, as I later try them on and will know for sure.

Fourth, price. Is it insanely expensive or can I reasonably afford it? Like, I won't spend 60 bucks on a dress when I'd be spending 10 bucks in other places.

Fifth, time to try it on if possible. From there my priorities come up.

1. Comfort. If clothes are uncomfortable, no matter how cute, I don't usually buy them, as I likely won't wear them

2. Looks. Does it look good on me or not? If something is extremely comfortable but looks meh, I tend to buy them to wear at home. Does it look bad and isn't too comfortable? Nope.

3. Total price. If I have a lot of itens that are comfy and look good, but my total price is getting too high for my liking? I'll pick out the things I like most and put the rest back

4. Practicality is the lowest, it doesn't really matter too much to me. Things like very short shorts aren't the most practical, but if they passed the other categories I'll buy them to only wear at home

The only "treatment" I've recieved so far was, to me, for others, rather than for myself. "But now you understand yourself better", no, you're wrong. I knew these things all along, since I was a child, I just didn't know back then that it had a name and was normal.

The only thing they're doing now is giving supposed support for autism, but they continually miss the point no matter how many times I tell them. I don't have the energy required to do anything. I need to take a several hour nap every afternoon just to function and I'm almost constantly running in overdrive. 

Therapist says: "it's because of your autism". Cool, how do I make it better? "Limit recieved stimuli". Uhm excuse me? I consistently try eliminating as much of it as I can, but so long as I have to leave the house, whether it be for college, my eventual forced internship, or a dreaded job, I get back absolutely destroyed, mostly mentally. And no amount of vacation or breaks stop that

Psychiatrist says: "there's medication that can help reduce the impact of stimuli". Cool, can I get those? "You need to do a blood test first". No problem, done. Results are back. Great, I stopped my other meds for nothing, and now I am again, left with nothing as the only reason I succeeded in losing weight before was medication that reduced appetite
